claims.text: velocity-history.md table (lines 9-15): Sprint 10-14 planned/velocity 10/8, 11/11, 7/6, 10/10, 11/9; Sprint 12 short-staffed (two developers on leave one week, team took in fewer points).

Lines 17-20: velocity varies so the team does not forecast from one sprint; the four full-staffed sprints (10, 11, 13, 14) lie in 8 to 11; Sprint 12 is not used as the low end for a full-staffed sprint and shows velocity drops with fewer people.
Forecast section (lines 22-30), made at Sprint 15 planning: 30 points left = 28 refund points + 2 carried over from Sprint 14; with all four developers, 8 to 11 points gives 3 to 4 sprints.

Lines 32-43: from Sprint 15 one of four developers does gateway integration and reconciliation, no point work; the other three do about three quarters, so 6 to 8 points; 4 to 5 sprints, 8 to 10 weeks from Sprint 15; redone each sprint planning.
velocity-history.md line 3: each sprint lasts two weeks.

Scrum Guide 2020, Sprint Planning: the more the Developers know about their past performance, their upcoming capacity, and their Definition of Done, the more confident they will be in their Sprint forecasts. ('Upcoming capacity means how much they can work' is the lesson's gloss.)
claims.source_hint: Scrum Guide 2020, Sprint Planning, Topic Two

claims.text: A forecast from the lowest and highest velocity of recent full-staffed sprints, as a range of sprints rounded up, is a more honest answer to 'when' than one date; an average hides the variation.

When fewer people are available, the team takes in less than its usual velocity instead of expecting others to cover; a forecast is redone at every sprint planning, and one kept unchanged tends to be treated as a promise.
